start.text:
You are the emergency department registrar on a morning shift.

Priya Nair, 28, is brought in by her partner. She is a physiotherapist presenting with a 2-day history of right-sided pelvic pain that worsened acutely an hour ago. She has had some light vaginal spotting since yesterday.

Her last menstrual period was approximately 7 weeks ago. She reports her periods are usually regular. She is not currently using contraception.

On first impression: she is pale, sitting hunched over, and appears uncomfortable. She rates her pain 6/10 at rest.

Vitals: HR 96 | BP 108/68 | RR 18 | SpO₂ 99% | Temp 37.1°C | Pain 6/10

What is your first priority?

choices.text: Order a urine pregnancy test immediately while taking a brief history

effects.reason: Urine pregnancy test ordered immediately — the single most important initial step in any woman of reproductive age with pelvic pain

choices.text: Take a full history before ordering any tests
Perform an abdominal examination immediately

effects.reason: Examination without first checking pregnancy status risks anchoring on musculoskeletal causes and delaying critical workup

choices.text: Administer analgesia first to make the patient more comfortable

effects.reason: Analgesia is appropriate but should not precede confirming pregnancy status in a woman of reproductive age with pelvic pain

history-and-hcg.text:
While the urine pregnancy test is being processed (result in ~5 minutes), you take a targeted history.

Priya tells you the pain started as a dull right-sided ache 2 days ago and has become much sharper over the last hour. It radiates to her right shoulder tip intermittently. She has had light brownish spotting but no heavy bleeding.

She has no urinary or bowel symptoms. She feels slightly lightheaded when standing.

What history would you like to focus on next?

choices.text: Detailed obstetric and gynaecological history (LMP, prior pregnancies, STI history)
Skip further history and wait for the urine pregnancy test result

effects.reason: OB history (LMP, prior pregnancies, STI risk) is essential to risk-stratify for ectopic pregnancy before the result is back

history-hub.text:
Priya is cooperative but uncomfortable. She reports right-sided pelvic pain, worsening over the last hour, with intermittent right shoulder-tip pain. Light vaginal spotting started yesterday. Her LMP was approximately 7 weeks ago.

What aspects of history do you want to explore?

choices.text: Obstetric and gynaecological history (LMP, prior pregnancies, STI history)
Order a urine pregnancy test now

effects.reason: Urine pregnancy test ordered — essential first step in any woman of reproductive age with pelvic pain

ob-history-detail.text:
Priya's OB/GYN history:

• G1P0 — one prior pregnancy ending in spontaneous miscarriage at 8 weeks, 2 years ago
• LMP: approximately 7 weeks ago; usually regular (28-day cycles)
• Not using contraception; actively trying to conceive
• History of pelvic inflammatory disease 3 years ago (treated with antibiotics)
• Chlamydia infection 4 years ago (treated)
• No known laparoscopic or tubal surgery
• No current IUD

She is not aware of whether she is Rh positive or negative.

This history significantly elevates your concern for ectopic pregnancy. You now have a clear picture of her risk factors.

What do you do next?

choices.text: Check the urine pregnancy test result (it should be ready)

effects.reason: Urine hCG ordered after history — good practice, though slightly delayed
Quantitative serum β-hCG ordered — essential for discriminatory zone interpretation

early-exam-node.text:
Abdominal examination:

• Abdomen soft, non-distended
• Marked tenderness in the right iliac fossa and suprapubic region
• Mild voluntary guarding in the right lower quadrant
• No peritonism on percussion
• Bowel sounds present

Pelvic examination (deferred — you choose not to perform it without knowing the pregnancy status first, which is appropriate).

The findings are consistent with a right adnexal process. You should now establish the pregnancy status before proceeding.

choices.text: Order a urine pregnancy test now

effects.reason: Urine hCG ordered — essential in any woman of reproductive age with pelvic pain

urine-hcg-result.text:
URINE PREGNANCY TEST RESULT
————————————————
Result: POSITIVE

Priya Nair is pregnant.

You now have a confirmed positive pregnancy test in a woman with:
• 7 weeks amenorrhoea
• Right-sided pelvic pain (acute worsening)
• Right shoulder-tip pain (possible diaphragmatic irritation from haemoperitoneum)
• Vaginal spotting
• Prior PID and chlamydia (major risk factors for ectopic)
• HR 96, BP 108/68 (borderline low)

Ectopic pregnancy must be excluded urgently. What do you do next?

choices.text: Order transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS) urgently and draw bloods (serum β-hCG, CBC, blood type)

effects.reason: TVUS ordered urgently — the definitive imaging modality for first-trimester pregnancy localisation
Quantitative serum β-hCG ordered for discriminatory zone interpretation
Rh blood type checked — essential for anti-D prophylaxis decision
IV access and bloods drawn — appropriate preparation for potential surgical emergency

choices.text: Order a transabdominal ultrasound (it's quicker to arrange)

effects.reason: Transabdominal ultrasound alone is insufficient for first-trimester evaluation — TVUS has significantly higher sensitivity for early ectopic and IUP localisation

choices.text: Reassure her this is likely a threatened miscarriage and discharge with GP follow-up

effects.reason: Discharging a haemodynamically compromised pregnant patient with risk factors for ectopic and acute pelvic pain without imaging is dangerous and contrary to evidence-based guidelines

choices.text: Call obstetrics immediately before any further workup

dangerous-discharge.text:
Priya is discharged home with a diagnosis of threatened miscarriage and advice to follow up with her GP in 3–5 days.

Six hours later, she returns by ambulance in haemorrhagic shock. She had a ruptured right fallopian tube. She required emergency laparotomy, salpingectomy, and 4 units of packed red blood cells.

A diagnosis of ectopic pregnancy was missed at the initial presentation.

This outcome reflects a failure to apply systematic clinical reasoning. In any pregnant patient with acute pelvic pain, risk factors for ectopic, and heamodynamic instability, ectopic pregnancy must be excluded with imaging before discharge — not assumed to be benign.

early-obs-consult.text:
You call the obstetrics registrar on-call. They are busy in theatre and advise you to complete the initial workup and call back with results.

They say: 'Get a TVUS and serum β-hCG and call me with the results. If she deteriorates haemodynamically, call me straight away.'

What do you do now?

choices.text: Order TVUS and serum β-hCG as advised, plus CBC and blood type

effects.reason: TVUS ordered urgently for first-trimester localisation
Quantitative serum β-hCG ordered
Rh type checked for anti-D decision
IV access established

taus-limited-result.text:
TRANSABDOMINAL ULTRASOUND REPORT
————————————————————
Uterus: Anteverted, non-gravid appearance. No definite intrauterine gestational sac identified.
Right adnexa: Possible heterogeneous area, difficult to characterise — limited view due to body habitus and early gestational age.
Left adnexa: Normal.
Pouch of Douglas: Cannot adequately assess for free fluid on this view.

REPORT: Inconclusive. Recommend transvaginal ultrasound for further evaluation.

As expected, the transabdominal ultrasound has not answered the question. TVUS is required. What do you do now?

choices.text: Order TVUS now (as recommended), plus serum β-hCG, CBC, and Rh blood type

effects.reason: TVUS ordered after inconclusive TAUS — recognised the limitation and escalated correctly
Serum β-hCG ordered
Rh type checked
IV access established

bloods-and-tvus-ordered.text:
You have ordered TVUS, serum β-hCG, CBC, and Rh blood type. The ultrasound technician will be with her in approximately 20–25 minutes. Blood results will take 30–45 minutes.

Priya is in the resuscitation bay. Her vitals just now: HR 102 | BP 102/64 | Pain 7/10.

Her blood pressure is trending down and her heart rate is trending up. You are concerned about haemodynamic compromise.

While waiting for imaging, what do you do?

choices.text: Establish large-bore IV access and start IV fluid resuscitation

effects.reason: IV fluid resuscitation initiated — appropriate supportive care while awaiting imaging

choices.text: Continue monitoring and wait for TVUS result before intervening further

resus-in-progress.text:
You have established IV access. 500 mL of normal saline is running. Priya's vitals stabilise slightly: HR 100 | BP 106/66.

The TVUS technician arrives. You need to be in the room for the result. What do you want to address before the scan?

choices.text: Call the obstetrics registrar to update them on the clinical picture

effects.reason: Obstetrics notified early — this is a potential surgical emergency requiring senior team involvement

choices.text: Go straight to the TVUS (you can call OB after you have results)

vitals-deteriorating.text:
URGENT: Priya becomes acutely more unwell.

Repeat vitals: HR 118 | BP 86/52 | RR 22 | SpO₂ 97% | Pain 9/10

She is pale, diaphoretic, and reports sudden severe lower abdominal pain. She is becoming lightheaded.

This is haemodynamic compromise. The clinical picture is consistent with a ruptured ectopic pregnancy with haemoperitoneum.

This is a surgical emergency. What do you do immediately?

choices.text: Crash call obstetrics, large-bore IV access x2, fluid resuscitation, type and cross-match, prepare for emergency theatre

effects.reason: Obstetrics called emergently — correctly recognised haemorrhagic shock and escalated to surgical team
IV resuscitation initiated in haemorrhagic shock

emergency-surgical-pathway.text:
The obstetrics team arrives immediately. Priya is taken to emergency theatre.

Intra-operatively: Right fallopian tube ruptured with 800 mL haemoperitoneum. Emergency right salpingectomy performed. Blood transfusion given intra-operatively.

Priya recovers in ICU overnight and is discharged on day 4.

Outcome: Ectopic pregnancy managed surgically following rupture. The diagnosis was delayed — earlier imaging and stabilisation would have allowed for safer planned intervention. The patient survived due to appropriate escalation when deterioration was recognised, but the delay to imaging was a missed opportunity for pre-rupture diagnosis and potentially laparoscopic (fertility-sparing) management.

tvus-result.text:
TRANSVAGINAL ULTRASOUND REPORT
————————————————————
Uterus: Anteverted, 8 × 5 × 4 cm. Endometrial stripe thickened (15 mm). No definite intrauterine gestational sac identified. No yolk sac or embryo within the uterine cavity.

Right adnexa: Heterogeneous ring-like structure (2.8 cm) adjacent to and separate from the right ovary — consistent with an adnexal mass. No cardiac activity identified within this structure.

Left adnexa: Normal. Left ovary unremarkable.

Free fluid: Small-to-moderate volume of echogenic free fluid in the pouch of Douglas and extending to the right paracolic gutter — consistent with haemoperitoneum.

IMPRESSION: No intrauterine pregnancy identified. Right adnexal mass with free haemoperitoneum. Findings are highly suspicious for RIGHT ECTOPIC PREGNANCY.

β-hCG (serum) is back: 4,200 mIU/mL — above the transvaginal discriminatory zone. A gestational sac should be visible with IUP at this level. None is seen.

This confirms the diagnosis. What is your management?

effects.reason: Ectopic pregnancy correctly identified on TVUS + β-hCG above discriminatory zone

choices.text: Call obstetrics urgently — this requires surgical or medical (methotrexate) management

effects.reason: Obstetrics consulted urgently with confirmed ectopic diagnosis

choices.text: Update the obstetrics registrar with these results — she is already aware
Administer methotrexate immediately without OB consultation

effects.reason: Methotrexate is NOT an emergency physician's decision to make unilaterally — it requires OB consultation, haemodynamic stability assessment, and specific criteria (no rupture, hCG < 5,000). With free fluid on scan, rupture must be excluded first.

premature-methotrexate.text:
You administer methotrexate without obstetric consultation.

The obstetrics registrar is called by nursing staff and arrives immediately. They review the ultrasound findings — the free fluid in the pouch of Douglas represents active haemoperitoneum. This patient has a RUPTURED ectopic pregnancy.

Methotrexate is contraindicated in ruptured ectopic pregnancy. The patient requires emergency surgery, not medical management.

Priya is taken emergently to theatre for laparoscopic salpingectomy. The delay caused by the methotrexate administration (and associated workup) added time to her definitive care.

This outcome reflects an important principle: methotrexate requires:
• Haemodynamic stability
• No evidence of rupture
• hCG < 5,000 mIU/mL (relative)
• OB/GYN consultation and consent
• Patient ability to follow up reliably

obs-management-decision.text:
The obstetrics registrar arrives in the ED. She reviews your workup and agrees with the diagnosis: right ectopic pregnancy with small haemoperitoneum.

Vitals now: HR 100 | BP 106/68 | Pain 7/10

She says: 'She is haemodynamically borderline. I want to take her to theatre for laparoscopy. She has free fluid on scan so methotrexate is not safe.'

Before she goes to theatre, what else do you need to address?

choices.text: Confirm Rh status and administer anti-D immunoglobulin (she is Rh negative)

effects.reason: Anti-D immunoglobulin administered to Rh-negative patient after pregnancy loss — prevents Rh sensitisation in future pregnancies

choices.text: Complete handover to the OB team — the patient is in good hands now

effects.reason: Anti-D immunoglobulin was not given before handover — the ED physician shares responsibility for this in an Rh-negative patient with bleeding in pregnancy

anti-d-given-node.text:
Anti-D immunoglobulin (250 IU) has been administered IM.

You complete a thorough handover to the obstetrics registrar. Priya is consented for emergency laparoscopy.

Anything else before she goes to theatre?

choices.text: Handover is complete. Accompany patient to theatre reception.

handover-without-anti-d.text:
Priya is taken to theatre for emergency laparoscopy. A ruptured right ectopic pregnancy is found and a right salpingectomy is performed.

Post-operatively, the obstetrics team notes that anti-D immunoglobulin was not given in the ED. They administer it post-operatively.

Priya recovers well and is discharged on day 3.

The outcome was good, but anti-D was a missed step. In Rh-negative women, sensitisation from an unrecognised pregnancy can cause haemolytic disease of the newborn in a future pregnancy — a preventable complication with a single IM injection.

outcome-excellent.text:
Priya Nair undergoes emergency laparoscopy.

Intra-operative findings: Right fallopian tube ectopic pregnancy with a small amount of haemoperitoneum (approximately 150 mL). The tube has not fully ruptured.

A right salpingotomy is performed, and the ectopic pregnancy is removed. Her left tube is intact and healthy.

She returns to the ward post-operatively in a stable condition, with good pain control and appropriate monitoring. She is discharged on day 2.

Priya is counselled about her future fertility, with explanation that her left tube remains intact. She is given a follow-up plan for serial β-hCG levels until they reach zero, to confirm complete resolution.

Your systematic approach — early pregnancy testing, urgent TVUS, serum β-hCG, Rh prophylaxis, and timely OB consultation — led to a near-optimal outcome. Excellent work.
